title: Rosetón
idiom: cathedral rose window: glass, leading, stone tracery, cast light
rule: One petal module (a lancet carrying a four-band resistor built out of its own glass) is drawn twelve times at 30 degrees; the colour permutation follows the resistor code applied to the first twelve digits of pi (3.14159265358), and the seventh petal is inverted - the break.

readings.far: a rose window: stone surround, radiating stone tracery, a jewelled outer ring of small lights, a grey centre
readings.middle: twelve lancets, each a four-band resistor in glass whose colours run orange, brown, yellow, brown, green, white, red, blue, green, orange, green, grey; a twelve-pin chip at the centre
readings.near: quarries subdivided by lead; gold circuit traces along the mullions with solder junctions; the stone's cast shadows on the glass assembling into a dove; the seventh petal with its widest band at the centre instead of the rim

techniques: one petal module x 12 at 30 degrees; the resistor code of pi's first twelve digits as the colour permutation
each lancet is a resistor: its four glass bands are the four colour bands
one petal inverted (bands mirrored, widest band at the centre) - the deliberate break
the tracery as a circuit: gold traces along the mullions, 24 solder junctions, a twelve-pin chip
quarries subdivided by lead so the glass reads as pieces, not paint
cast stone shadows clipped to the glass, forming a dove only at 100%
flat glass colour; grain as the final layer
statement: A rose window wired like a resistor network. Its twelve lights are the first twelve digits of pi in the resistor code - a palette no glazier would choose - and the stone between them is a circuit with a twelve-pin chip at its heart. The shadows the tracery throws on the glass are not uniform: from outside, they are a dove.
